title: Lateral Movement
summary: Lateral movement is the progression from one compromised system or identity to others inside the same environment, performed to reach valuable data, higher authority, or a position from which the final objective can be achieved without returning to the internet. It rarely relies on a novel exploit; most real intrusions reuse credentials, sessions and administrative tooling that already exist. Typical mechanisms include interactive remote access over desktop, terminal or remote management protocols, authenticated file sharing and remote service creation, execution frameworks that push jobs to many machines at once, and control-plane operations in cloud or virtualisation platforms that reach many workloads through a single API. Credential reuse drives much of it, whether the material is a plaintext password, a password hash, a cached ticket or a long-lived API key, and it is frequently shared service accounts and duplicated local administrator passwords that make the movement cheap. Detection depends on joining authentication events to host and network context: a workstation authenticating to another workstation, an account logging in from a system it never normally touches, remote service or scheduled task creation, and east-west traffic that crosses a segmentation boundary. Mitigations reduce the number of usable hops rather than the number of alerts: segmented networks with default-deny rules between tiers, unique local administrator credentials, dedicated privileged access workstations, just-in-time administration, and removal of legacy authentication protocols. In cloud estates the same logic applies to role assumption paths and to network reachability between workloads.
objectives: You will be able to explain why lateral movement is dominated by credential reuse rather than exploitation.
You will be able to identify the authentication and host telemetry that reveals movement between systems.
You will be able to describe how segmentation, administrative tiering and unique local credentials reduce reachable paths.
You will be able to interpret east-west network flow data to spot traversal across trust boundaries.
You will be able to trace a role-assumption chain in a cloud tenant as a form of lateral movement.

beginner.definition: Lateral movement is the step where an intruder moves from one compromised machine or account to another inside the same network. They do this to reach valuable data, gain higher authority, or find a better position. It rarely needs a brand new software flaw. Most of the time it reuses existing passwords, sessions and admin tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: One stolen laptop should not unlock the whole company. But in many networks, one password works on many machines. Shared admin accounts and repeated local passwords make movement cheap for an intruder. If you cannot see logins between your own systems, you cannot follow the path they take. Network segmentation, which splits a network into smaller parts, limits how far a single password reaches.
howItWorks: The intruder starts on one machine they already control with a low-level account.
They search the machine for stored passwords, saved sessions and admin tools.
They try those credentials on other systems, often using normal remote access features.
When one works, they repeat the process from the newly reached machine.
Step by step, they approach systems that hold the data or rights they want.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building where every door uses the same key. A cleaner loses their key ring at the bus stop. The person who finds it can open the reception, then the finance office, then the server room. Each door feels safe on its own, but the shared key joins them all together. In networks, reused passwords and shared admin accounts are that same key ring. One small loss becomes a path through the building.
takeaways: Attackers usually move sideways with stolen credentials, not new exploits.
Give every machine its own unique local administrator password, not one shared one.
Log and review the logins that happen between your own internal systems.

exercises.title: Lateral Movement - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Lateral Movement - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Lateral Movement - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Lateral Movement - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
